name: Epics, Songs and Silver Screens: India's Storytellers
description: From the Ramayana and the Mahabharata to Bollywood and the films of Satyajit Ray: how India has told its stories in verse, stone, song and film.

checkpoints.name: The great epics
checkpoints.note: The Ramayana and the Mahabharata, both composed over centuries, carry tales of exile, war and duty that are still told across India and much of Asia. The Bhagavad Gita, a dialogue set inside the Mahabharata, becomes one of the best-known texts of Hindu thought.

checkpoints.name: Courts and monuments
checkpoints.note: Kalidasa's play Abhijnanashakuntalam, from around the fifth century, is among the best-loved dramas in Sanskrit. Under the Mughal Empire, which begins in 1526, the Taj Mahal is built from 1632 and largely finished by about 1653, while in Amritsar the Golden Temple becomes the holiest shrine of the Sikhs.

checkpoints.name: Press and poetry
checkpoints.note: The Times of India, founded in Bombay in 1838, is one of the oldest newspapers still printed. Rabindranath Tagore, born in 1861, writes poems, songs and plays in Bengali, and in 1913 becomes the first person outside Europe to win the Nobel Prize in Literature.

checkpoints.name: Talkies and new waves
checkpoints.note: The first Hindi talking film arrives in 1931, and Bollywood grows up in the studios of Bombay. India is partitioned in 1947. Satyajit Ray's Pather Panchali (1955) wins praise abroad, Mother India (1957) is a huge hit, and the singer Lata Mangeshkar and the sitar player Ravi Shankar become known around the world.

checkpoints.name: Blockbusters and television
checkpoints.note: Sholay (1975) becomes one of the best-loved adventure films in India. The television serial Ramayan (1987) draws enormous audiences, Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge (1995) plays for years in a Mumbai cinema, and Lagaan (2001) is nominated for an Academy Award.
